adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/mixins/issues.py:390 — When two linked issues share an integration, an inbound assignment from one suppresses updates to both and leaves the other issue out of sync.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that when two linked issues share an integration, an inbound assignment from one suppresses updates to both. However, looking at the diff, the check at line 390 compares `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id`. This check is per-installation/per-external-issue, not global. Each external issue has its own GroupLink and would be processed separately. The sync_assignee_outbound task is called per external_issue_id (see sync_group_assignee_outbound in utils/sync.py), and each call would have its own installation context. The finding misunderstands how the sync cycle prevention works - it prevents syncing back to the SAME integration that triggered the change, not to all integrations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/models/groupassignee.py:138 — The core GroupAssignee manager now depends on an integrations-layer AssignmentSource solely to relay provenance through several layers, coupling every assignment caller to issue-sync plumbing.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the GroupAssignee model manager (a core model layer) now imports and accepts AssignmentSource from the integrations layer. Looking at the diff, line 15 adds 'from sentry.integrations.services.assignment_source import AssignmentSource' to groupassignee.py, and the assign/deassign methods now accept 'assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None' parameters. This creates a dependency from the core models layer to the integrations layer, which is a legitimate architectural concern about coupling. The parameter is optional (None default), so it doesn't break existing callers, but it does introduce a cross-layer dependency that a reviewer might want to discuss.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:16 — source_name and queued are serialized across the task boundary but never read in production, needlessly enlarging and version-coupling the wire contract beyond the integration_id used for cycle prevention.

adjudication.rationale: The finding is accurate - looking at the diff, AssignmentSource has three fields (source_name, integration_id, queued) that are serialized via to_dict() and passed through the task boundary in sync_assignee_outbound. However, examining the code that uses the deserialized AssignmentSource, only integration_id is actually used (in should_sync() to check sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id). The source_name and queued fields are serialized but never read in the production code paths shown. This is a valid architectural concern about unnecessary data being passed across task boundaries, though it's not a bug since the code functions correctly.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/mixins/issues.py:416 — The assignee-specific AssignmentSource was added to the unrelated sync_status_outbound abstract API despite having no status caller or implementation consumer, creating dead cross-feature coupling.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that `assignment_source` parameter was added to `sync_status_outbound` abstract method signature (lines 408-417), but examining the diff, there's no implementation that uses this parameter and no caller that passes it. The parameter is named `assignment_source` which is assignee-related terminology being added to a status sync method. This is a valid architectural concern - the parameter appears to be added preemptively or incorrectly to an unrelated method. However, this could also be intentional preparation for future work. The finding correctly identifies that the parameter is added but not used in this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:18 — Evaluating timezone.now() as a dataclass default gives every source created by a process the same stale queued timestamp, making queued-time metadata incorrect.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` as a default value in a dataclass field at line 18 of assignment_source.py. In Python, default values for function/method parameters and dataclass fields are evaluated once at definition time, not at call time. This means `timezone.now()` is called once when the module is loaded, and all AssignmentSource instances created without explicitly passing a `queued` value will share that same stale timestamp. This is a well-known Python gotcha and represents a real bug where the queued timestamp will be incorrect for all instances after the first one.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py:221 — The new test covers only same-source suppression, so it would not catch a regression that blocks assignment propagation to a different linked integration.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a gap in test coverage. The new test `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` only tests the case where the assignment source matches the target integration (same integration_id), verifying that sync is blocked. However, there's no test for the scenario where an assignment comes from one integration and should propagate to a different linked integration. The new logic in `should_sync` (lines 388-391 in mixins/issues.py) checks `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id` to prevent cycles, but the test suite doesn't verify that assignments from different integrations still propagate correctly. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for newly added logic.
